newsitem.title: CHINA: China dissident asks leaders for 'right to exist'.
newsitem.headline: China dissident asks leaders for 'right to exist'.

text.p: Veteran Chinese dissident Qin Yongmin said on Friday he had appealed to President Jiang Zemin to end official persecution, for the chance to run his own small business and for the right to exist.
"I want to survive... I want to live," Qin said in a telephone interview from his home in Wuhan, capital of the central province of Hubei.
"I hope that President Jiang can solve my problems," said Qin, who was jailed for two years in 1994 for joining several dissidents in writing a peace charter advocating peaceful political reform.

Qin said he had posted his appeal to Jiang on Thursday evening in a desperate attempt to try to improve his circumstances after local authorities announced they would tear down his small bookshop in Wuhan.
"The government firstly won't let me go abroad and secondly won't let me leave Wuhan," he wrote in the daring appeal. "But you should give me at least one route to survival.

"I'm damned if I do and damned if I don't," he wrote. "So I can only write to the President of the People's Republic of China and ask you to take pity on me, give me a road to life and guarantee my right to existence."

Qin, who has been demanding democracy for China since the Democracy Wall movement of the late 1970s and who spent several years in jail in the 1980s, said he had been running a small bookshop since his release from prison in late 1995.

However, local authorities have notified Qin and his neighbours that they plan to demolish the row of shops to widen the street and to make way for new development, with the buildings due to be torn down within days, he said.
"I don't know whether this is directed against me," said Qin, who is in his late 40s. "But it means that I will have no way to earn a living and I have invested all my money in this shop."

He said he was demanding the authorities compensate him by giving him a similar amount of space in the new building to be built on the same site. He decided to take his appeal to the president and Communist Party chief after local officials ignored his pleas.

"The government has stressed time and again that the right to survival and development are the most important human rights, hence I have no choice but to write to you about my right to exist after coming under persecution," he said in his letter to Jiang.

Qin last angered the authorities when he and eight other activists drafted a "peace charter" in Beijing in November 1994 that called for non-violent change and cooperation with China's hardline communist government.
Qin ran up against the authorities in 1993 after he publicly opposed China's bid for the 2000 Olympics, saying the country was too poor to host such a huge event.
He was detained in Wuhan and freed on September 24, 1993, a day after the International Olympic Committee announced Sydney had won the games.
His appeal came just a day after families of students killed in China's June 4, 1989, crackdown on dissent flocked to cemeteries in Beijing to mourn their loved ones.

China's authorities routinely boost security nationwide around the anniversary of the crackdown, when troops backed by tanks moved into Beijing's Tiananmen Square to crush weeks of student-led pro-democracy demonstrations, killing hundreds.
